extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors reporting in vivo animal experiments, journal editors and peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for transparent reporting of in vivo animal studies (ARRIVE-style): what information to include about methods, timing, rationale, results, background, objectives and ethical approval to allow reproducibility and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9b When and how often.
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly report the frequency and timing of experimental procedures and measurements, including light/dark cycle, circadian time cues, and experimental time sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include details such as light and dark cycle (e.g. 12L:12D), circadian cues (e.g. lights on at 08:00), intervals between baseline and comparator measurements, and intervals between procedures and measurements. Report timing and frequency of welfare assessments considering normal activity patterns (see item 15 – Animal care and monitoring), because circadian rhythms and timing can affect behavioural, physiological and immunological outcomes. If timing varies between animals, supply a supplementary table listing times for each animal. Examples: • ‘Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and amount of blood extracted were recorded every 5 minutes. Blood samples drawn at baseline, 0, 30 and 60 minutes.’ • ‘After a 5-h fast (7:30–12:30am), awake mice were randomized and subjected to three consecutive clamps with 2 days recovery between clamps.’

rubrics_metrics.name: 9c Where (including detail of any acclimatisation periods).
rubrics_metrics.description: State where studies were performed and whether physiological or procedural acclimatisation periods were included, with type and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe location(s) (dedicated lab space, animal facility, home cage, behaviour arena, water maze, etc.), whether physiological acclimatisation after stressful events (e.g. transport) was provided and its duration, and whether procedural acclimatisation immediately before procedures occurred. Note that physiological acclimatisation can take from 24 hours to more than a week depending on species/strain/outcome; procedural acclimatisation helps stabilise responses after handling or novel environments. If multiple sites were used, explicitly state where each experiment and sample analysis was performed. Include any laboratory accreditation if relevant (e.g. commercial labs). Examples: • ‘Fish singly housed 1 week before habituation; conditioning tank habituation over 2 days…each fish placed in apparatus for 20 minutes then returned to home tank.’

rubrics_metrics.name: 9d Why (provide rationale for procedures).
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why particular procedures or techniques were chosen, especially when approaches are novel, lab-specific, or constrained by the animal model or equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the scientific or practical rationale for chosen methods (e.g. route of administration determined by animal size). Explain why the approach is best suited to the question, and justify deviations from common practice. This is particularly important when methods could bias results or when multiple approaches exist. Examples: • Choice of intraperitoneal injection of 18F-FDG because murine tail veins are too small and partial paravenous injection would bias biodistribution comparisons. • Rationale for targeting C-terminus of X. laevis Ctnnb1 for epitope tagging based on previous evidence that C-terminal tags do not affect function.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10a Summary/descriptive statistics for each experimental group, with a measure of variability where applicable (e.g. mean and SD, or median and range).
rubrics_metrics.description: For each experiment and independent replication, report descriptive statistics for each group including a measure of variability and the exact number of experimental units per group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide measures of central tendency and variability appropriate to the data (mean ± SD, median and range, quartiles, etc.). Report results for all experiments conducted (including repeats), not just representative experiments. State exact sample sizes so readers can assess reliability (see item 2 – Sample size, and item 3 – Inclusion and exclusion criteria). Present data clearly as text, tables, or graphs to enable evaluation and extraction for meta-analysis. Examples include reporting means ± SD with ranges in brackets, and using boxplots (median and IQR) with whiskers showing percentiles. The guideline stresses reporting all collected data and choosing visualisations that reveal distribution (e.g. boxplots).

rubrics_metrics.name: 10b If applicable, the effect size with a confidence interval.
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effect sizes with confidence intervals to indicate magnitude and precision of observed effects, alongside or instead of relying solely on p-values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain biological significance beyond statistical significance; include effect size and its confidence interval to indicate precision. Report all analyses performed, including non-significant results. Effect sizes facilitate interpretation, especially when power is low or hypothesis-testing is inappropriate, and aid systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Examples: • Standardised genotype effect with 95% CI shown per sex; significant estimates highlighted. References and discussion note that p-values are influenced by sample size and that confidence intervals provide essential information about effect magnitude and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11 Abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accurate summary of research objectives, animal species, strain and sex, key methods, principal findings, and study conclusions in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure abstracts are transparent and accurate because they are used as screening tools and can determine inclusion in systematic reviews. Include species, sex, strain, methods and results, and clearly state whether the study was hypothesis-testing or exploratory (see item 13 – Objectives). Avoid inconsistencies between abstract and full text. A well-composed abstract enables readers to judge study relevance and reliability; omitting species or intervention names limits the utility for systematic reviews. Examples: structured BACKGROUND/EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH/KEY RESULTS/CONCLUSIONS example given for asthma murine study and a pig housing study.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12a Include sufficient scientific background to understand the rationale and context for the study, and explain the experimental approach.
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide background that demonstrates the evidence gap and explains why an in vivo approach is warranted, and outline how the experimental approach addresses the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relevant references and, when available, cite systematic reviews of animal literature to justify the question and choice of model. Describe prior work, limitations of previous models, and how the current approach fills the evidence gap. Explain how the approach relates to existing research and why it is appropriate to answer the question. Examples include justification for developing disease-representative animal models when clinical failures indicate shortcomings of common models.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12b Explain how the animal species and model used address the scientific objectives and, where appropriate, the relevance to human biology.
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough detail to assess suitability of the animal model for the research question and, where relevant, its validity relative to human disease or biology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include rationale for species choice, explain how outcome measures are relevant to the condition studied, and describe model validation. Do not rely on statements that a model is ‘commonly used’ without further justification. When modelling aspects of human disease, indicate how induction, response to known treatments, symptom similarity, and selection of animal characteristics (age, sex, health status) make the model appropriate. Examples: pilocarpine model of epilepsy chosen because it recapitulates human temporal lobe epilepsy features; zebrafish transplantation models justified by conserved haematopoietic mechanisms and imaging advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13 Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly describe the research question(s), research objectives and, where appropriate, specific hypotheses being tested, and state whether the study is exploratory or hypothesis-testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish exploratory from confirmatory (hypothesis-testing) aims because this affects design, analysis, sample size calculations and interpretation. For hypothesis-testing studies, prespecify primary outcome measures and provide a priori sample size estimation. For exploratory studies, acknowledge multiple outcomes and higher false-positive risks. Clearly identify which hypotheses were prespecified and which arose after data inspection. Examples: primary and secondary objectives stated for immune response and functional outcomes in MSC implantation study; exploratory calcium electroporation study described as exploratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14 Ethical statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the name of the ethical review committee or equivalent that approved the study and any relevant licence or protocol numbers, or justify why approval was not sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how the study conforms to applicable regulations and guidelines, name the approving institution/committee (e.g. IACUC, AWERB), and include protocol or project licence numbers for identification. Mention any accreditation (e.g. AAALAC, GLP) where appropriate. If formal ethical approval was not required (e.g. species not regulated), provide a clear justification and cite relevant international standards to demonstrate compliance. Examples include explicit statements of UK Animal (Scientific Procedures) Act compliance with project licence numbers, or descriptions of local regulatory determinations that formal review was unnecessary.
